en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on Vessantara, Concerning the Question of Inference.
9. The Question on Nibbāna as Exclusive Happiness “Venerable Nāgasena, is Nibbāna exclusively happy, or is it mixed with suffering?
“It is exclusively happy, Great King; Nibbāna is unmixed with suffering.”
“Venerable Nāgasena, we do not believe that statement, ‘Nirvāṇa is exclusively blissful.
Rather, Venerable Nāgasena, we conclude in this matter that ‘Nirvāṇa is mixed with suffering,’ and we perceive a reason here why ‘Nirvāṇa is mixed with suffering.’”
What is the reason for this?
Venerable Nāgasena, those who seek Nibbāna are seen to exert and strain both body and mind;
they observe standing, walking, sitting, lying down, and food; and they suppress drowsiness and [restrain] the sense bases.
It is an oppression characterized by the abandonment of wealth, grain, dear ones, and friends.
Whatever beings in the world are happy or endowed with happiness, they all delight and nourish themselves with the five strands of sensual pleasure in their sense bases;
they delight and nourish the eye with forms that are variously beautiful, whether pleasing or unpleasing.
They delight and nourish the ear with sounds characterized by various beautiful signs—both pleasing and unpleasing—such as singing and instrumental music;
they delight and nourish the nose with odors characterized by various beautiful signs—both pleasing and unpleasing—such as flowers, fruits, leaves, bark, roots, and heartwood;
[they delight and nourish the tongue] with flavors characterized by various beautiful signs—both pleasing and unpleasing—such as food to be chewed, swallowed, licked, drunk, and tasted.
They delight and nourish the tongue with taste; they delight and nourish the body with tactile contact that is agreeable or disagreeable, soft, subtle, mild, gentle, and manifold beautiful signs;
they delight and nourish the mind with mental attention to thoughts that are agreeable or disagreeable, auspicious or inauspicious, beautiful or ugly, and manifold.
You are destroying, damaging, cutting, severing, obstructing, and stifling that which nourishes the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

Because of this, the body is tormented and the mind is tormented; when the body is tormented, one experiences bodily painful feeling, and when the mind is tormented, one experiences mental painful feeling.
Does not even the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya, while censuring the Blessed One, say: “The ascetic Gotama is a destroyer of beings”?
“This is the reason here, by which I say that ‘Nibbāna is mixed with suffering.
“Indeed not, Great King; Nibbāna is not mixed with suffering; Nibbāna is exclusively blissful.
As for what you say, Great King, ‘Nibbāna is suffering,’ that is not suffering; it is called Nibbāna.”
But this is the preliminary stage for the realization of Nibbāna; it is the quest for Nibbāna.
Nibbāna, Great King, is exclusively blissful; it is not mixed with suffering.
I shall state the reason for this.
“Is there, Great King, such a thing as what is called the pleasure of kingship?
“Yes, venerable sir, there is the pleasure of kingship for kings.
“But is that pleasure of kingship, Great King, mixed with suffering?”
“No indeed, Bhante. “But why, Great King, do your kings, when the border regions are in revolt,
go forth on an expedition surrounded by ministers, generals, mercenaries, and soldiers to suppress those border-dwellers, even while being oppressed by gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, and heat?”
“They run about on even and uneven ground, engage in great battles, and encounter danger to their very lives.
“This, venerable Nāgasena, is not what is called the happiness of kingship; this is merely the preliminary stage in the pursuit of the happiness of kingship.
It is through suffering, venerable Nāgasena, that kings pursue and then experience the happiness of kingship.”
“Even so, venerable Nāgasena, the happiness of sovereignty is unmixed with suffering; that happiness of sovereignty is one thing, and suffering is another.
“In the same way, Great King, Nibbāna is absolute happiness; it is not mixed with suffering.
But those who seek that Nibbāna, having afflicted their bodies and minds through standing, walking, sitting, lying down, and fasting,”
Having mastered themselves, suppressed sloth, and constrained the sense bases; having sacrificed both body and life and sought nibbāna through suffering,
they experience the absolute bliss of nibbāna, just as kings who have subdued their enemies enjoy the happiness of sovereignty.
“Thus, Great King, Nibbāna is exclusively blissful, unmixed with suffering; Nibbāna is one thing, and suffering is another.
Furthermore, Great King, hear another further reason why Nibbāna is exclusively blissful, unmixed with suffering, and how suffering is one thing and Nibbāna is another:
Great King, do teachers who possess crafts not have what is called the ‘bliss of the craft’?”
“Yes, venerable sir, there is the craft-happiness of teachers who possess crafts.
“But, great king, is that craft-happiness mixed with suffering?
“No indeed, venerable sir.”

“But why, Great King, do your teachers torment their bodies by bowing down and rising up for their teachers; by fetching water, sweeping the house, providing tooth-sticks and water for rinsing the mouth;

by receiving their leftovers, covering them with robes, bathing them, and massaging their feet; and by setting aside their own minds to conform to the minds of others, enduring painful beds and irregular meals?”
“Venerable Nāgasena, this is not what is called the happiness of a craft; rather, this is the preliminary stage of seeking a craft.
Venerable Nāgasena, it is through suffering that teachers seek a craft and subsequently experience the happiness of that craft.
Thus, venerable Nāgasena, the happiness of a craft is unmixed with suffering; the happiness of the craft is one thing, and the suffering is another.”
“In the same way, Great King, Nibbāna is exclusively blissful and is not mixed with suffering.
Yet those who seek that Nibbāna do so by tormenting their bodies and minds, by restricting themselves to standing, walking, sitting, lying down, and food,
by suppressing sleep, by constraining the sense bases, and by sacrificing both body and life.”
“Having sought Nibbāna through suffering, they experience the absolute bliss of Nibbāna, just as teachers experience the joy of their craft.
Thus, Great King, Nibbāna is absolute bliss; it is not mixed with suffering. Suffering is one thing, and Nibbāna is another.
“It is well, venerable Nāgasena! It is so; I accept it as you have said.”
The ninth question: On Nibbāna as Absolute Bliss.
